  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 53

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Visual (Weapons): Weapons or objects used as weapons, Trauma-Related Events: Trauma-related events, Conflict: Confrontations
  Memory: Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief, Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory

Vignette:
Ana Morales had always taken pride in her work as a cybersecurity analyst. She was meticulous and thorough, with an eye for detail that served her well in identifying potential threats to her company's systems. But on one fateful day, three years ago, Ana's precision failed her. During a training exercise at the police department where she worked part-time, Ana accidentally fired a live round from a handgun, seriously injuring her partner. The memory of that moment was etched into Ana's mind like a scar. She recalled the sound of the gunshot, the smell of smoke and sweat, and the sight of her partner's bloodied uniform. But there were gaps in her recollection too - moments she couldn't quite piece together no matter how hard she tried. What happened in those missing seconds haunted her still. In the aftermath of the accident, Ana became consumed by grief whenever she remembered that day. The pain was so intense it felt like a physical blow, leaving her breathless and disoriented. Her colleagues at work began to notice changes in her behavior - she would become withdrawn and isolated during meetings, or zone out when discussing security protocols. Ana tried to avoid anything that might trigger those memories: she stopped attending training exercises, turned down invitations from friends who were police officers, and even avoided news reports about gun violence. But it was the visual cues that really got to her - seeing a handgun, either in real life or on TV, would send her spiraling back into the depths of that traumatic day. At work, Ana's avoidance behaviors took a toll on her performance. She started missing deadlines and struggled to focus during meetings. Her usually sharp mind was clouded by anxiety and fear of being confronted with another potentially traumatic situation. When colleagues asked her questions about security threats, she'd freeze up, unable to articulate the concerns swirling in her head. Ana's partner had been more than just a colleague - he was also a close friend. His death left a void in Ana's life that seemed impossible to fill. Even three years on, the grief still felt overwhelming at times. Sometimes, when driving home from work or during quiet moments alone, Ana would be hit with a wave of emotion without any clear image or memory attached - just an intense sense of loss and regret. Ana's husband had been her rock in those dark days following the accident. But he passed away suddenly six months ago, leaving Ana feeling lost and adrift once more. With no one to confide in, she began to feel like she was drowning under the weight of her secrets and fears. One evening, as she stared blankly at her computer screen, Ana realized that something needed to change. She couldn't keep living in a state of perpetual avoidance and fear. The anxiety had started seeping into every aspect of her life - even simple tasks felt like insurmountable challenges. That's when she knew it was time to seek help. Ana scheduled an appointment with a therapist, hoping to find a way out of the darkness that seemed to have swallowed her whole. She feared being forced to confront those painful memories all over again, but something inside her whispered that maybe - just maybe - there was a chance for redemption and healing on the other side.
